title: One to One Relationships & Inner Joins
summary: Introduces relational design in Postgres through the simplest relationship, one to one, using student and contact_detail tables linked by a primary key / foreign key pair. Shows how an INNER JOIN with ON combines the two tables into one wide result.

concepts.heading: Why relationships matter
points: Linking tables is the main strength of SQL databases; the next three lessons cover one to one, one to many and many to many.
Relationships are usually planned on a crow's-foot (ER) diagram first. Free tools like draw.io let you draw tables, fields and the links between them.

concepts.heading: One to one relationship
points: One row in table A maps to at most one row in table B. Here one student has one contact_detail row.
Common motive is modularity: databases cope well with very many rows but get unwieldy with very many columns, so rarely-used or grouped columns can be split into a second table.
The student table holds first_name, last_name and an id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY (auto-incrementing from 1). contact_detail holds tel and address (e.g. for contacting parents).

concepts.heading: Linking with a foreign key
points: contact_detail.id is declared INTEGER (it must match the type of the student primary key) and REFERENCES student(id). REFERENCES marks the column as a FOREIGN KEY pointing at student's primary key.
UNIQUE on that column stops the same student id appearing twice in contact_detail, which is what enforces the one-to-one rule (without it you would get one to many).
(Extra) Postgres also rejects inserting a contact_detail row whose id does not exist in student, which is referential integrity.
The PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies rows within its own table; the FOREIGN KEY identifies which row in another table a record belongs to.

concepts.heading: Inserting related data
points: Insert the student first. Because id is SERIAL, the first student gets id 1.
Then insert into contact_detail using that same value (1) as the foreign key, plus a made-up phone and address.
Insert order matters: the referenced row must exist before the row that points at it.

concepts.heading: INNER JOIN
points: SELECT * FROM student JOIN contact_detail ON student.id = contact_detail.id returns one wide row combining both tables' columns.
JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides appear.
ON states the matching rule, here primary key equals foreign key. Table-qualified names (student.id) are needed because both tables have a column called id.
The result has columns from student first, then contact_detail, so id shows twice.

concepts.heading: SQL comments and setup
points: SQL comments start with two dashes (--) and are ignored when run, used to label sections in queries.sql.
Download the lesson resources (Family Travel Tracker starter) which include queries.sql with all the lesson's statements, to copy rather than retype.

task.name: Build the school database and run the one-to-one join
task.starting_point: Resources zip containing queries.sql with all statements for the next three lessons; pgAdmin connected to your server.
task.goal: Create a school database, build the student and contact_detail tables, insert linked data and join them.
steps: In pgAdmin collapse existing databases, create a new database named school and save.
Open the Query Tool on school.
Paste and run the two CREATE TABLE statements; refresh Schemas > Tables to confirm both exist.
Run the INSERT statements from the Data section: first the student, then the contact_detail row using id 1.
Run the SELECT ... JOIN ... ON query and confirm one combined row with all five fields appears.
task.expected_result: A single result row: id, first_name, last_name, id, tel, address for Angela Yu.

solution_code.code:
SELECT *
FROM student
JOIN contact_detail
ON student.id = contact_detail.id

task.reference_repo_path: Section 33 - PostgreSQL/33.11 - One to One Relationships & Inner Joins/queries.sql

pitfalls: Forgetting UNIQUE on the foreign key silently allows many contact rows per student.
Mismatched column types between primary and foreign key.
Inserting the child row before the parent exists.
Running the join in the wrong database (check the Query Tool is on school).
